title: Netflix Is the Only Streaming Company Actually Making Money. The Market Punished It Anyway.
subtitle: A Q2 earnings beat met with a 7% selloff. $13.6B in net income, $11.2B in free cash flow, 325M subscribers, and an ad business tripling in a year — yet the stock trades near two-year lows. The disconnect is this generation's media mispricing.
summary: Netflix reported a beat in Q2 and got sold off for it — down 7% on July 17 despite record revenue, record margins, and $11.2B in trailing free cash flow. At 18x forward P/E with 50% ROE, a $20B content engine, and an ad tier that tripled to 250M MAUs in a year, the market is pricing the only profitable streamer like a declining media company. The structural moat hasn't been this mispriced since the 2022 washout.

image.caption: Netflix's content catalog and global scale form a structural moat competitors can't replicate.

bodyHtml:
Let's get one thing straight: Netflix just reported one of the best quarters in its history. Record revenue. Record margins. Record free cash flow. A booming ad business that's doubling faster than anyone predicted. And the market responded by selling off the stock like the company was heading for bankruptcy.

Shares cratered more than seven percent the day after Q2 earnings dropped — on a beat, by the way. That's not a typo. Net income of $13.6 billion over the last twelve months, $11.2 billion in free cash flow, 33% operating margins, and the stock gets punished. The forward P/E is down to about 18 times for a company growing revenue 13% and producing returns on equity around 50%. Half a percent of return on every dollar of equity. And the market is pricing it like a legacy TV network that's bleeding subscribers.

So what happened? Netflix reported July 16. EPS of $0.80, a whisper above the $0.79 consensus. Revenue tracking toward $48 billion for the year. Subscriber growth still humming — 325 million global paid members and counting. And the stock dropped the next day like it was bad news. The narrative was that the ad ramp is priced in, subs are plateauing, and competition from Disney and Warner Bros. Discovery is finally going to bite. It doesn't hold up.

Here's what the pessimists are missing. Netflix has a structural moat nobody else in streaming can touch. A $20 billion content engine operating across 190 countries, producing everything from Korean survival dramas to French thrillers to Nigerian rom-coms — local content that global audiences actually watch. That's not something you build overnight. That's not something you buy. That's a decade-plus head start in data, taste, and production relationships, and the gap is widening.

The ad business is the real unlock. Netflix's ad tier has ballooned to 250 million monthly active users — roughly triple where it was a year ago at about 94 million. The company is targeting $3 billion in ad revenue for 2026 and projecting $5 billion by 2027. Think about that. In less than two years, advertising could add a revenue stream larger than the entire annual revenue of most mid-cap media companies. And the margins are dramatically higher than subscription-only revenue because the marginal cost of an ad impression is basically zero once the content exists.

Meanwhile, the competitive field is a graveyard. Disney+ is still losing hundreds of millions per quarter. Max hasn't turned a real profit. Paramount+ is bleeding cash. Peacock has lost well over $8 billion since launch. Every one of them is subsidizing streaming losses with declining linear TV cash flows — a model with an expiration date. Netflix, by contrast, operates at 33% margins with $11 billion in free cash flow. They're not just winning the streaming war. They're the only ones who figured out how to monetize at scale.

Let's talk about valuation because that's where things get funny. Eighteen times forward earnings for a business with 50% returns on equity and double-digit revenue growth. The S&P 500 trades around 22 times with much lower ROE. The market is saying Netflix is riskier than the average S&P company — which is absurd. Netflix has a $20 billion content war chest, 325 million subs who absorb price increases without churning (three hikes in three years, minimal impact), and a second revenue engine in ads that's barely getting started.

The bears will tell you subscriber growth is tapped out. But 325 million households is a long way from a billion-plus at pay-TV's peak. Netflix is still in early innings across Asia, Africa, and Latin America. Every new subscriber in those markets comes with content costs already sunk — the marginal economics only get better.

Here's the bottom line. Netflix is the only streaming company with the scale and business model to print cash in any environment. Pricing power competitors envy. A content engine nobody can replicate. An advertising business that doubles revenue per user without doubling costs. The stock has been cut nearly in half on concerns that don't survive contact with the actual numbers. At some point, the market will wake up and realize it's been pricing a declining media company when what it actually owns is the dominant global entertainment platform of the next decade. When that re-rating happens, the current price is going to look like one of the easiest layups on the board.

Disclosure: The Signal holds no position in NFLX. Positions may change. This is not financial advice.
